question: A 16-year-old with PPRP has an equinovarus foot. You plan tendon transfer to correct the deformity. Which of the following is the most important prerequisite before performing a tendon transfer?

answers.text: The donor muscle must have power grade ≥3 on the MRC scale

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Grade 3 (movement against gravity only) is insufficient. A muscle loses approximately one grade after transfer; a grade 3 donor becomes grade 2 post-operatively and will not provide useful function.

answers.text: The donor muscle must have power grade ≥4 on the MRC scale

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The cardinal rule: donor muscle must be at least grade 4 (movement against gravity plus resistance). After transfer, one grade is lost, leaving grade 3 — the minimum for functional active movement.

answers.text: All joint deformities must be corrected after the transfer, not before

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wrong order. Fixed deformity must be corrected BEFORE tendon transfer. Transferring onto an uncorrected deformity results in the transferred tendon acting as a deforming force, worsening the problem.

answers.text: Triple arthrodesis should be performed simultaneously to provide a stable base

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Triple arthrodesis must wait until skeletal maturity (≥12–14 years for girls, ≥14–16 years for boys) to avoid causing growth arrest. It is not performed simultaneously with tendon transfer in a skeletally immature patient.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the tendon transfer prerequisites: donor grade ≥4, deformity corrected FIRST, and triple arthrodesis deferred until skeletal maturity. These three rules together define safe surgical planning in PPRP.
Well done. The minimum donor grade of 4 (MRC) is a non-negotiable rule — losing one grade post-transfer means a grade 4 donor delivers grade 3 function, the floor for useful active movement.
